title: The Vatican Museums’ 1932 spiral is two ramps wound together, so up and down never meet
body: In 1932 Pope Pius XI opened a new entrance to the Vatican Museums, with a staircase by the architect Giuseppe Momo. To climb the 22 m from the street to the level of the Vatican Gardens, a pit shaped like a truncated cone was dug into a bastion of the old walls, and in it wind **two ramps of 94 m each, one for visitors going up and one for those coming down**, as the opening booklet put it ([quoted by the museums’ director](https://www.museivaticani.va/content/dam/museivaticani/pdf/eventi_novita/Area_stampa/Rassegna_stampa/2020/40_portone_simbolo_apertura.pdf)). The second ramp starts half a turn round from the first, so at any point of the wall the floors alternate, and the two streams pass above and below each other. The price: with the other ramp overhead, each must climb twice its headroom every turn. Strictly the ramps are [conical spirals](https://www.iemest.eu/life-safety-and-security/images/Doc/ARTICOLI/2016/dipaola_26/FrancescoDiPaola01.pdf), as the pit narrows downwards. It is often called the Bramante Staircase, but Donato Bramante’s ramp, begun by 1512 for Pope Julius II, is a single spiral for horses and mules. Today the 1932 stair is the museums’ way out.

slides.question: Giuseppe Momo’s 1932 staircase at the Vatican Museums climbs from the street up to the museum level. How many metres?
slides.explanation: 22 m, in a pit shaped like a truncated cone. 15,000 m³ of earth were dug out for it, the booklet of 1932 says.

slides.alt: Animation in Art Deco green and bronze: a funnel-shaped pit 22 m deep, in which an amber ramp going up and a blue ramp coming down wind half a turn apart as walkers pass. A cut shows the floors alternating; then Bramante’s single ramp with 36 columns, and Orvieto’s double well.

slides.prompt: Wind two ramps up the 22 m shaft and find the most turns, the gentlest slope, that still leaves 2.2 m of headroom. Then try one ramp.
slides.takeaway: With two ramps, the other passes halfway between your floors, so 4 turns is the most here: a 15% slope. One ramp alone could make 8 turns at 7%. A double helix pays for its two streams in steepness.

slides.alt: Looking down Giuseppe Momo’s spiral staircase in the Vatican Museums: grey stepped ramps with white edges wind down between ornate bronze balustrades to a round floor far below, with a few visitors on the ramps and green marble on the wall.
slides.caption: Giuseppe Momo’s staircase from the top: its bronze balustrades spiral down into the pit.

left.label: Often said
left.text: The famous double spiral in the Vatican Museums is Donato Bramante’s, of the early 1500s.

right.label: In fact
right.text: The double spiral is Giuseppe Momo’s, 1932. Bramante’s ramp, begun by 1512 in a tower of the Belvedere, is one spiral with 36 columns.

slides.heading: Spirals for going up and down

events.text: Donato Bramante’s single spiral ramp is begun for Pope Julius II.
Orvieto’s well gets two spiral ramps for donkeys, one down, one up.
Pope Pius XI opens the museums’ entrance with Momo’s two ramps.
A second entrance opens beside it.

slides.question: In Giuseppe Momo’s 1932 staircase, why must each ramp climb twice its headroom on every turn?
options: The other ramp runs between its floors
The pit narrows towards the bottom
The ramps are made of steps
slides.explanation: Half a turn after your ramp passes a point of the wall, the other ramp passes it. So the floor above your head belongs to the other ramp, half a turn’s climb up.

source.label: Vatican Museums: the entrance of 1932 (L’Osservatore Romano, 2020)
